newsitem.title: SPAIN: Champagne flows as Spain toasts 20-year democracy.
newsitem.headline: Champagne flows as Spain toasts 20-year democracy.

text.p: Champagne flowed and politicians exchanged fond memories on Sunday as Spain celebrated the 20th anniversary of its first free elections after nearly 40 years of military dictatorship.

Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar laughed and joked with past and present politicians and clapped along to songs in a Congress jubilee to mark Spain's dramatic evolution from dictatorship to full-fledged democracy in just two decades.
"The great historic achievement of transition exists as a point of reference so that we do not forget and we never again commit the errors that have been committed during our history," Aznar said.

Little more than 20 years ago, Spain was still stifled by the grip of General Francisco Franco's rightist dictatorship, when opposition leaders were frequently arrested and jailed and the press was monitored and controlled.

But after Franco's death in December 1975, his successor King Juan Carlos opted for free elections and Spain soon found itself steaming down the road to democracy, eagerly shaking off its isolated Iberian past.
Since then, Spain has thrown open its doors to the outside world and staked a place among the first tier of European nations, political analysts say.

A far cry from Franco's strict autocracy, Spain has become one of Europe's most decentralised countries and boasts an enviable economy eager to claim a spot among the founders of a European single currency in 1999.

"There are few examples in recent history of countries which have demonstrated such economic and political vigour as Spain has and that makes us very proud to be Spanish and to have contributed to what is today an incredible democractic reality," said Economy Minister Rodrigo Rato.
After the death of Franco, many expected Juan Carlos to impose a Francoist monarchy as intended by the old dictator.
But the king surprised Spain by opting for democracy and called elections for June 15, 1977, the first since 1936.
The elections whipped up a fury of excitement as citizens celebrated their newfound freedom and turned up at the ballot boxes in droves.
"I was 62 and it was the first time in my life that I had the right to vote. It was the first time I had placed a vote in a ballot box," said former Communist Party leader Santiago Carrillo.
Adolfo Suarez, who became the first prime minister after the fall of the dictatorship, steered Spain in its first steps toward democracy.
His efforts secured him a place as the most popular of Spain's post-Franco prime ministers, a recent poll showed.
Calvo Sotelo took over as prime minister when Suarez resigned in 1981 and ruled until Socialist Felipe Gonzalez won a 1982 election.

After 13 years of Socialist rule, the election of Aznar's conservative Popular Party in 1996 marked a significant swing back to the right, a shift that political analysts interpreted as a sign that Spain's democracy had reached true maturity.
"The moment of change has arrived. This is the moment of normal democracy, of the alternation of power," Aznar, a former tax inspector, said after being elected.
